prompt:
Write an essay of about 1,500 words on whether primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.

text:
Every few years someone declares that handwriting is finished, and every few years the claim sounds a little more plausible. Children now meet keyboards and touchscreens before they meet pencils, adults hardly write anything longer than a shopping list, and a crowded primary curriculum has little room for skills that seem to belong to the age of the fountain pen. Joined-up handwriting, in particular, looks like an easy thing to drop. It is slow to teach, hard to master, and apparently irrelevant to a world of autocorrect. I think that view is mistaken. Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting, not out of nostalgia, but because it remains one of the most efficient ways of helping young children become fluent, confident writers.

The case against deserves a fair hearing first. Several American states removed cursive from their standards after the Common Core reforms, and Finland has moved toward keyboard instruction in the early years. The argument runs that time is finite, that typing will dominate adult life, and that the hours spent on looping letters would be better used on coding, reading, or typing itself. There is also a fairness point. Children with weak fine motor control can find joined writing humiliating, and a teacher who marks neatness can leave a bright but clumsy child feeling stupid. These are real concerns, and any defence of joined writing has to answer them rather than wave them away.

The strongest reason to keep it is simple fluency. Writing by hand is still the main way that children in school record and organise their thinking, and it will remain so for years to come. Most examinations are still handwritten, as are most classroom tasks in the primary years, when a school can rarely give every child a reliable device. A child who forms each letter separately must lift the pencil after every stroke, and that constant stopping and restarting costs time and effort. Joined writing lets the hand move in a continuous flow, so that whole words become single movements. The practical result is that a child who has mastered it can usually write faster and tire less, which leaves more attention for the content of what they are trying to say.

That matters because handwriting is not a separate skill sitting beside composition; it competes with it for the same limited mental resources. A young writer who must think hard about how to form a letter has less capacity left for choosing a word, building a sentence, or remembering the point they started with. Research on early writing, much of it by Virginia Berninger and her colleagues, has found that children who write more fluently tend to produce longer and better compositions. Automatic letter formation frees working memory for ideas. I do not claim that joined writing is the only route to fluency, since plenty of people write quickly in a tidy print. But a joined hand is the most natural way for most children to reach speed, and it is the one that teachers have the longest experience of teaching well.

There is also a case that joined writing helps with spelling and with the sense of a word as a unit. When a child writes a word in a single flowing movement, the sequence of letters is practised as a pattern, much as a pianist practises a phrase rather than a string of separate notes. Teachers often report that children who learn common letter strings as joined movements, such as the endings of past-tense verbs, spell them more reliably. The evidence here is thinner than enthusiasts sometimes suggest, and I would not rest the argument on it. Still, it fits what we know about motor memory, and it is at worst harmless. Joined writing also tends to fix a problem that print makes worse, which is uneven spacing between letters and words. Because the letters in a joined word are physically connected, children cannot scatter them across the line, and the gaps between words become easier to see and to judge.

Some of the most interesting research concerns the difference between handwriting and typing for learning. Studies using brain imaging, including work by Karin James and later Norwegian researchers, suggest that writing by hand engages the brain's networks for reading and memory more strongly than pressing keys does. Pre-literate children who practise forming letters by hand seem to recognise them more readily than those who only type them. Other studies have found that students who take notes by hand tend to process lecture material more deeply than those who type. This literature is contested, and some of the headline results have proved harder to replicate than their first reports implied. It would be foolish to claim that a pencil makes children cleverer. Nevertheless, the broad pattern is consistent enough to give a cautious school a reason for keeping handwriting at the centre of early literacy, instead of treating it as an optional extra.

Then there is the question of children who struggle. The fear that joined writing penalises the clumsy is fair, but I think the evidence points the other way for many of them. Teachers who work with dyslexic children have long favoured a joined hand, because it removes the common confusion between letters like b and d that look alike when printed in isolation. In a joined style, each letter begins and ends in a characteristic way, and the b and the d are formed with different movements that the hand can learn. A child who finds the shapes hard to distinguish on the page may find them easier to distinguish in the fingers. That is not a universal truth, and some children will always do better with print or a keyboard. The answer, though, is to support them individually, and not to withdraw the skill from everyone.

A wider cultural argument also deserves a modest place. Joined writing is the script in which most of the written record of the last few centuries was made. Letters, diaries, wills, registers, and annotated books are overwhelmingly cursive, and a generation that cannot read it will need translators to reach its own family history. American teachers and archivists have already reported students who struggle to read founding documents in their original form. A child who has learned to write joined letters can read them too, since reading and writing a script strengthen each other. A signature is a smaller example. Most adults still need to sign their names, and a signature that is a personal, practised, joined mark is harder to forge and easier to produce than a laborious string of capitals.

The strongest objection remains the time budget, so it is worth being concrete. Teaching joined writing well does not take an enormous share of a primary school week. In England, where the national curriculum expects pupils to move to a joined style in the early years, a few short, focused practice sessions each week are enough for most children to be fluent by the end of Key Stage Two. The cost is small, and the alternative is not free either. Children who never receive systematic teaching do not stop writing by hand; they develop idiosyncratic, inefficient habits that teachers must then try to repair, usually without the time to do it. It is better to teach a sound method early than to leave each child to improvise a poor one.

None of this means schools should teach handwriting badly. The worst version is a rigid regime that makes seven-year-olds trace copperplate for an hour and treats a messy page as a moral failing. A better approach teaches print first, introduces simple joins once letter formation is secure, and aims at a legible and reasonably quick personal hand, not a calligraphic ideal. Teachers should mark children on whether their writing can be read, and on what it says, and not on how elegant it is. They should allow children with genuine motor or perceptual difficulties to use other methods without stigma. And they should teach keyboard skills as well, because the two are not rivals. A child who can write fluently by hand and type competently is better equipped than one who can do only one.

That last point is the heart of the matter. The choice is not between the pencil and the keyboard, as the more excited commentators suggest, but between a curriculum that gives children both tools and one that quietly drops the older one. The older tool is not obsolete. It is cheap, silent, durable, and always available, and it requires no battery, no password, and no wifi. It lets a six-year-old make a mark on paper in the same moment as having a thought. Until every classroom, exam hall, and kitchen table has changed beyond recognition, children will keep needing to write by hand, and they will write better if someone has taught them how.

So the sensible position is a conservative one. Joined-up handwriting should stay in the primary curriculum, taught briefly and kindly, with the aim of fluency rather than beauty. It saves effort, supports other literacy skills, opens the written past, and costs little. The best argument for dropping it is that nobody needs it any more, but plenty of people still do, and the children who learn it will be glad of it for the rest of their lives.
